```{r}
library(duckdb); library(DBI); library(scales)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb(),
  here::here("../cabarrus-data-pipeline/db/cabarrus.duckdb"),
  read_only = TRUE)
cab  <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM nc_population_growth WHERE GEOID = '37025'")
n_nc <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM nc_population_growth")$n
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

<p class="topic-eyebrow">Population Analysis</p>

Between 2000 and `r cab$data_year`, Cabarrus County grew by `r round(cab$pct_growth)`%, adding more than `r comma(round(cab$abs_growth, -3))` residents to reach a population of `r comma(cab$pop_recent)`. That growth rate ranks `r scales::ordinal(cab$rank_growth)` among all `r n_nc` North Carolina counties. More telling than the raw rank is the spatial pattern: a Getis-Ord Gi* hot spot analysis confirms that Cabarrus is not an isolated spike but the core of a statistically significant regional growth cluster encompassing Mecklenburg, Union, and Iredell counties. The forces driving this growth, Charlotte's economic expansion and Cabarrus's relative affordability, show no structural sign of reversal.
